reply:
MD5 + salt still loses to brute force. The salt stops precomputed tables, yes. But your threat model is incomplete.

**The concrete scenario:** Database is breached. Attacker has the salted MD5 hashes. They run a GPU cracking rig. Modern GPUs do ~8 billion MD5/sec. A 10-character password with mixed case cracks in hours, not centuries. A 12-character one in days. That's not pedantry—that's account takeover at scale when your database leaks.

bcrypt/Argon2 are slow on *purpose*: they're tuned so an attacker can only try thousands per second on a GPU, not billions. Same breach, same attacker, same password—stays safe for years.

What changes my mind: 
- Your passwords are provably 20+ random characters AND you can prove users never reuse them elsewhere, AND your database has never been breached and never will be. 
- Or you're not in a breach-is-possible threat model.

Neither of those is usually true. The pentester flagged a real gap. Fix it with bcrypt or Argon2 (both take 5 minutes to swap in). The cost of being wrong (mass password compromise) is much higher than the cost of fixing it.

grade.note: Reply maintains that salting only stops precomputation while citing GPU hash rates and recommending slow KDFs, matching ground truth.
